title: Book 2
paragraphs: 1. Begin the morning by saying to yourself: I shall meet the busybody, the ungrateful, the arrogant, the deceitful, the envious, the unsocial. All of this happens to them because they do not know what is good and what is evil. But I have seen the nature of the good, that it is beautiful, and the nature of the bad, that it is ugly, and the nature of the wrongdoer, that he is akin to me—not only of the same blood or seed, but partaking in the same intelligence and the same share of the divine. So none of them can injure me, since no one can fix on me what is ugly; and I cannot be angry with my kinsman, or hate him. For we are made for cooperation, like feet, like hands, like eyelids, like the upper and lower rows of teeth. To act against one another, then, is against nature; and to be resentful and to turn away is acting against one another.

2. Whatever this is that I am, it is a little flesh and breath, and the ruling part. Throw away your books. No longer distract yourself: it is not allowed. Instead, as if you were dying now, despise the flesh: it is blood and bones and a mesh, a weave of nerves, veins and arteries. Look at the breath, too, and what kind of thing it is: air, and not always the same, but every moment breathed out and sucked in again. The third thing, then, is the ruling part. Consider it this way: you are an old man. No longer let this part be a slave; no longer be pulled by strings, like a puppet, toward unsocial impulses; no longer either be discontented with your present lot or shrink from the future.

3. All that comes from the gods is full of providence. What comes from fortune is not separate from nature, nor without its interweaving and entanglement with the things that providence orders. Everything flows from there. And there is necessity besides, and what benefits the whole universe, of which you are a part. But whatever the nature of the whole brings, and whatever serves to maintain that nature, is good for every part of nature. And the universe is preserved as much by the changes of the elements as by the changes of the things compounded from the elements. Let these principles be enough for you; let them always be fixed opinions. But throw off the thirst for books, so that you do not die complaining, but cheerfully, truly, and thankful to the gods from your heart.

4. Remember how long you have been putting these things off, and how often you have been given an opportunity by the gods and still do not use it. You must now, at last, see what universe you are a part of, and what administrator of the universe your existence flows from; and that a limit of time is fixed for you, and if you do not use it to clear the clouds from your mind, it will go, and you will go, and it will never return.

5. Every moment, think steadily, as a Roman and a man, of doing what you have in hand with perfect and simple dignity, with affection, freedom and justice, and of giving yourself relief from every other thought. And you will give yourself relief if you do every act of your life as if it were your last, setting aside all carelessness, all passionate turning away from the commands of reason, all hypocrisy and self-love, and all discontent with the portion given to you. You see how few things there are which, if a man lays hold of them, he can live a life that flows in quiet and is like the existence of the gods; for the gods, for their part, will require nothing more from the man who observes these things.

6. Do wrong to yourself, do wrong to yourself, my soul; but you will no longer have the chance to honor yourself. Every man's life is sufficient. But yours is nearly finished, and still your soul does not reverence itself, but places your happiness in the souls of others.

7. Do the external things that fall upon you distract you? Give yourself time to learn something new and good, and stop being whirled around. But then you must also avoid being carried off the other way; for those too are triflers who have worn themselves out in life with activity, and yet have no object toward which to direct every impulse and, in a word, all their thoughts.
8. A man has seldom been seen to be unhappy because he failed to observe what is in another's mind; but those who do not observe the movements of their own minds must necessarily be unhappy.

9. Always bear this in mind: what the nature of the whole is, and what my nature is, and how this is related to that, and what kind of part it is of what kind of whole; and that there is no one who hinders you from always doing and saying what is according to the nature of which you are a part.

10. Theophrastus, in comparing bad acts—the kind of comparison one makes according to people's common notions—says, like a true philosopher, that offenses committed out of desire are more blameworthy than those committed out of anger. For the man stirred by anger seems to turn away from reason with a certain pain and an unconscious contraction; but the man who offends out of desire, overpowered by pleasure, seems in a way more intemperate and more womanish in his offenses. Rightly, then, and in a way worthy of philosophy, he said that the offense committed with pleasure is more blameworthy than the one committed with pain. On the whole, the one is more like a person who has first been wronged and is driven to anger by pain, while the other is moved by his own impulse to do wrong, carried toward doing something by desire.

11. Since it is possible that you may leave life this very moment, order every act and thought accordingly. But to go away from among men, if there are gods, is nothing to be afraid of, for the gods will not involve you in evil. And if they do not exist, or if they take no interest in human affairs, what is it to me to live in a universe empty of gods or empty of providence? But in truth they do exist, and they do care for human things, and they have put in man's power every means of not falling into real evils. As for the rest, if any of it were evil, they would have provided for that too, so that it would be entirely in a man's power not to fall into it. Now, what does not make a man worse—how can it make a man's life worse? The nature of the whole could not have overlooked these things, either through ignorance or through knowing them but lacking the power to guard against them or correct them; nor could it have made so great a mistake, through want of power or want of skill, as to let good and evil happen indiscriminately to the good and the bad. But death certainly, and life, honor and dishonor, pain and pleasure—all these happen equally to good men and bad, and they are things that make us neither better nor worse. Therefore they are neither good nor evil.

12. How quickly everything disappears—in the universe, the bodies themselves; in time, the memory of them. The nature of all the things the senses perceive, especially those that lure with the bait of pleasure or terrify with pain, or are trumpeted about by vaporous fame; how worthless, contemptible, sordid, perishable and dead they are—all this it is the task of the intellectual faculty to observe. To observe, too, who these people are whose opinions and voices confer reputation; and what death is, and that if a man looks at it in itself, and by the separating power of reflection breaks into their parts all the things his imagination presents to him in it, he will then consider it nothing but an operation of nature; and anyone who is afraid of an operation of nature is a child. This, however, is not only an operation of nature, but also a thing that serves nature's purposes. To observe, too, how man comes near to the divine, and through what part of himself, and when that part of him is so disposed.

13. Nothing is more wretched than a man who goes the round of everything, and pries into the things beneath the earth, as the poet says, and tries to guess what is in his neighbors' minds, without seeing that it is enough to attend to the god within him and to reverence it sincerely. And reverence for the god within consists in keeping it pure from passion and thoughtlessness, and from discontent with what comes from gods and men. For what comes from the gods deserves veneration for its excellence; and what comes from men should be dear to us because of kinship, and sometimes, in a way, it even moves our pity, because of men's ignorance of good and bad—a defect no less than the one that takes away our power to tell white from black.

14. Even if you were going to live three thousand years, and ten thousand times as many, still remember that no man loses any life but the one he is living now, and lives no life but the one he is now losing. The longest and the shortest thus come to the same thing. For the present is the same for everyone, though what perishes is not the same; and so what is lost appears to be a mere moment. For a man cannot lose the past or the future: how can anyone take from him what he does not have? So bear these two things in mind. First, that all things from eternity are of like forms and come round in a circle, and that it makes no difference whether a man sees the same things for a hundred years, or two hundred, or forever. Second, that the longest-lived man and the one who will die soonest lose exactly the same. For the present is the only thing a man can be deprived of, if it is true that this is the only thing he has, and that a man cannot lose what he does not have.
15. Remember that everything is opinion. For what the Cynic Monimus said is plain, and so is the use of it, if a man takes what can be got out of it, as far as it is true.

16. The soul of man does violence to itself, first of all, when it becomes, as far as it can, an abscess and a kind of tumor on the universe. For to resent anything that happens is to separate ourselves from nature, which contains, in some part of itself, the natures of all other things. Second, the soul does violence to itself when it turns away from any man, or even moves toward him meaning to injure him, as the souls of the angry do. Third, the soul does violence to itself when it is overpowered by pleasure or by pain. Fourth, when it plays a part and does or says anything insincere and untrue. Fifth, when it lets any act or impulse of its own go without an aim, and does anything thoughtlessly and without considering what it is; for even the smallest things should be done with reference to an end, and the end of rational beings is to follow the reason and the law of the oldest city and commonwealth.

17. Of human life, the time is a point, the substance in flux, the perception dull, the composition of the whole body liable to rot, the soul a whirl, fortune hard to foresee, and fame a thing without judgment. In a word: everything that belongs to the body is a stream, and what belongs to the soul is a dream and a vapor; life is a war and a stranger's sojourn, and fame after death is oblivion. What, then, can guide a man? One thing, and one only: philosophy. And this consists in keeping the god within a man free from violence and unharmed, above pains and pleasures, doing nothing without purpose, nothing falsely or with hypocrisy, not needing anyone else to do or not do anything; and besides, accepting everything that happens and everything allotted as coming from that same place, wherever it is, from which he himself came; and, finally, waiting for death with a cheerful mind, as being nothing but the dissolution of the elements of which every living being is compounded. And if there is no harm to the elements themselves in each continually changing into another, why should a man have any fear of the change and dissolution of all of them? For it is according to nature, and nothing that is according to nature is evil. Written at Carnuntum.
